missions.title: The Label on the Blade
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What can a pattern on the surface tell us about how something was made, and what can it not tell us?
missions.stake: If the market keeps believing the loudest voice, Corvan's 'ancient' blade sets the prices, and families pay for a story.

objectives.title: Arrive in Emberford, a guild town in Aethelgard.
Find out what the trader Corvan claims about his patterned blade.
Follow the blade's Provenance Thread: Corvan's stall, the guild ledger, the Lyle workshop.
At Hesper's anvil, forge a small test billet. Cut it and compare it at the assay table.
Face Corvan in a Showdown in the market square about his sign.
Talk to Hesper about what happened in the market.
Meet Kip by the portal stone.
Go back through the portal stone and show the seal to Warden Ise.

missions.title: The Copy in the Square
missions.knowledgeQuestion: Who has heard a claim, and who still needs to hear its correction?

objectives.title: Trace the old order. Read the guild entry, the workshop slip and Sefa’s packet.
Choose how to get a correction to the people who took the old slips.
Carry the dated copy to the south gate, or meet Hana at the west stall for the spoken handover.

cards.title: Corvan's sign
cards.text: Corvan's sign says: 'True wootz of ancient Damascus. 24 marks.'
cards.limits: A seller's description is a claim. It is not a record of how the blade was made or where it came from.

cards.title: Hesper's workshop sheet
cards.text: Hesper's sheet for this blade: layers of two different steels stacked, forge-welded, twisted and folded, then shaped and etched. Dated this season.
cards.limits: This is the maker's own record. It does not say where her steel stock came from.

cards.title: Assay cross-section of the blade (schematic)
cards.text: The assay table's etched cross-section of an offcut from the blade shows separate welded layers that follow the folds.
cards.limits: In this game it is a schematic illustration, not a real micrograph. A trained assayer would need to confirm it.

cards.title: Guild ledger entry
cards.text: Emberford guild ledger: one patterned blade sold by the Lyle workshop to Corvan Hale, this season.
cards.limits: The ledger records a sale. It does not describe the steel.

cards.title: Your test billet: pattern welded
cards.text: You stacked, welded and folded two steels. The cut face shows light and dark layers that follow the folds, with thin weld lines. The blade's section shows the same kind of thing.
cards.limits: Hesper's forge in this game is schematic, not a working recipe. One billet is one case.

cards.title: Your test billet: crucible cake
cards.text: You melted iron in a sealed pot and let it cool. The cut face shows soft bands with no weld lines. It does not match the blade's section.
cards.limits: Schematic only. Real crucible steel needs exact materials and great skill, which the game does not show. It cannot tell you how any real wootz looked.

cards.title: Ten wootz steel ingots (Met record)
cards.text: The Metropolitan Museum of Art catalogues 'Ten Wootz Steel Ingots with Bag', accession 2023.133a–k, as Indian, probably eighteenth century.
cards.limits: The word 'probably' is part of the record. These are ingots, the raw material, not finished blades.

cards.title: Met essay on techniques
cards.text: The Met's essay on decorating arms and armour separates pattern welding, which joins and works different iron or steel pieces, from crucible or 'watered' steel.
cards.limits: An essay about techniques does not identify any particular blade.

cards.title: Two kinds of 'Damascus'
cards.text: A 1998 experimental study by Verhoeven, Pendray and Dauksch uses both 'pattern-welded Damascus' and 'wootz Damascus'. So 'Damascus' alone does not name one recipe.
cards.limits: The study examines particular wootz blades. It says nothing about blades sold in Emberford.

exhibits.name: Patterned blade on Corvan's stall
exhibits.dateKind: A SELLER'S CLAIM, not a date from any record. Nothing on the stall says when or where it was made.
exhibits.summary: A blade with a wavy, layered surface pattern. In this game world it was made in Emberford. It is NOT a historical object and has no ancient provenance.
exhibits.altText: A short steel blade with a flowing grey pattern of light and dark bands on its surface.

exhibits.name: Ten Wootz Steel Ingots with Bag (catalogue record, Met 2023.133a–k)
exhibits.dateKind: A CATALOGUE DATE with a qualifier. 'Probably' means the museum is not certain. Keep the qualifier.
exhibits.summary: Sefa's catalogue shows the record of a real group of ten wootz steel ingots with a bag, catalogued by The Metropolitan Museum of Art as Indian, probably eighteenth century.
exhibits.altText: A catalogue page showing ten small rounded dark metal cakes next to a cloth bag.

exhibits.name: Assay table: etched cross-section of the blade
exhibits.dateKind: A PREPARATION DATE: when this test sample was cut and etched.
exhibits.summary: An offcut from the same billet as Corvan's blade, cut and etched by the guild assayer. The drawing is schematic. Bring your own cut billet here to compare.
exhibits.altText: A small polished steel slice with bands of light and dark layers that bend along folds.

threads.title: The blade's Provenance Thread

nodes.label: Corvan's stall
nodes.text: Corvan holds the blade now. His sign hangs above it. Kip shields the chalk with a sleeve. “When it rains, who will remember whose words those were?”

nodes.label: Guild ledger
nodes.text: The guild ledger lists a sale from the Lyle workshop to Corvan this season. Kip traces the column with his nail. “My aunt gets paid on that date. It could sit on the shelf a year first.”

nodes.label: Lyle workshop
nodes.text: Hesper has dated her workshop sheet this season. “If somebody brings this back, I need the day it left my hands.” Her date and the clerk’s happen to match. One records her work, the other a sale.

gap.text: Past the workshop the thread goes dark. Nobody recorded where Hesper's two steels came from. That part of the story is missing, and you should say so.

threads.limit: The thread shows who held the blade and who wrote it down. It cannot show what is inside the steel, or anything that nobody recorded.

showdowns.title: Market Showdown: the sign on the blade
showdowns.intro: A buyer folds her purse shut. Hesper stands at the edge of the fountain. Corvan smooths a crease in his father’s sign.

links.text: The watery pattern shows that it is wootz.
links.cracked: A pattern can come from welded layers. Your own billet made one, and the blade's section shows weld lines that follow folds.
links.holds: This card does not touch what a pattern can show.

links.cracked: The guild ledger and the workshop sheet both date the blade to this season.
links.holds: This card does not give a date for the blade.

links.text: Steel with this look is called Damascus, so it comes from Damascus.
links.cracked: 'Damascus' names more than one kind of steel. The word alone does not name a place or a recipe.
links.holds: This card does not show what the word 'Damascus' can mean.

counterexamples.why: Your own billet has the same kind of pattern, and you made it this week in Emberford.

opponentClaim.sourceReply: Corvan: 'Source? The pattern is the source! And the mark on my sign.' He taps a gold corner on the sign. There is nothing written under it.

playerClaims.text: Corvan is a cheat and the blade is a fake.

supports.why: The sheet shows who made the blade. It does not show that anyone meant to cheat, and the blade is real steel.
One billet is one case. It cannot speak for every blade.

playerClaims.text: This blade is pattern-welded, made in Hesper Lyle's workshop this season.

supports.why: An independent record of the sale, this season.
The blade's own section shows welded layers.
Your billet shows how welded layers look when cut.

playerClaims.text: A pattern on the surface alone cannot show that a blade is wootz.

supports.why: The Met separates pattern welding from crucible steel.
'Damascus' is used for both kinds of steel.
Your crucible cake had a pattern too, of a different kind.
Real wootz is a crucible-steel tradition with its own records.

playerClaims.reframe: Corvan's sign is about this one blade. Your claim is about what any pattern can show. Every buyer in the square needs the second answer too.

witnesses.name: Hesper Lyle
witnesses.line: I made that blade, this season, in my forge. Two steels, welded and folded. I am proud of it, and it is not wootz.

witnesses.name: Guildmaster Orrin
witnesses.line: The ledger records the sale: Lyle workshop to Corvan Hale, this season. I keep the ledger; I do not judge steel.

witnesses.name: Sefa Okon
witnesses.line: A pattern on the surface does not prove that a blade is wootz. The songs say so too: 'look at the hand, not the shine'.

fairPoints.text: Corvan: 'I paid a fair price for it, and I have a family to feed. I did not make the blade.'
fairPoints.concede: You agree: Corvan paid fairly and did not make the blade. The crowd softens.

fairPoints.text: Corvan: 'It is good steel. Look at it!'
fairPoints.concede: You agree: it is good steel and good work. Hesper nods from the forge road.

script.line: Corvan taps a small gold mark in the corner of his sign: 'This sign carries a mark of quality. Ask anyone.'
Corvan: 'And what is under YOUR claim, Guardian?'

exposed.text: Corvan takes down the sign. Two buyers ask for refunds. Hesper steps beside him to help find their receipts.

narrowed.text: Corvan writes “Lyle workshop, this season.” He dips the brush again. “May I keep the bit about good steel?”

won-over.text: Corvan leaves room below his own name. Hesper takes the brush. The first letter wobbles. He holds the board steady.

split.text: Half the square drifts away. Corvan keeps his sign and pins “Maker: Lyle workshop” where a child can read it.

lost-ground.text: The gold sign draws the crowd. Nobody opens a purse. Hesper saves you a dry corner of the workshop sheet for tomorrow.

testimony.line: Corvan, to the crowd: 'My supplier swore on his name: this blade came out of an old tomb near Damascus. Centuries old!'
testimony.caught: The guild ledger and Hesper's sheet record this blade as made this season, here in Emberford. A sworn story does not outweigh a dated record. The crowd murmurs.
testimony.wrong: That card does not touch what Corvan just said. Which card puts a date on this blade?

journal.text: At the bench I found Hesper’s repair tab beside the Nexus receipt. Hesper showed me which face she had promised to mend. Her apprentice kept the forge open in Emberford.
In the Nexus drawer I found Hesper’s repair tab next to a separately dated receipt. Anyone at the counter could ask for the pair while the shop finished its work.
Arrived in Emberford, a guild town in Aethelgard. Aethelgard is a game world: nothing here is a historical record unless it says 'Documented'.
Corvan's sign says his blade is 'true wootz of ancient Damascus'. He bases it on the pattern.
The Provenance Thread ran from Corvan's stall to the guild ledger to the Lyle workshop. Then it went dark: nobody recorded where the steel stock came from.
I forged a test billet and cut it. At the assay table I compared my section with the blade's section. A pattern alone does not tell you the route.
I faced Corvan in the market square. Some links in his claim broke; the crowd watched what held up.
Kip found a small gold seal on the back of Corvan's old sign. Lumen does not know the mark. What I know: it was there. What I do not know: who put it there, or why.
Back in the Nexus. Warden Ise went quiet when she saw the seal. Hesper Lyle says she will visit 'to see how you people test things'.
We sent the correction with the order number. People could match it to the copy they already had. The workshop’s public name travelled with it and the private names stayed inside.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: Guardians! Look at this. True wootz of ancient Damascus. See the water in the steel? Only twenty-four marks. That gold stamp gets my price onto the order slips. Once a buyer takes a copy, the order desk uses my description too.

options.text: How do you know it is wootz?
Where did you get it?
Nice pattern.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: The pattern! Everyone knows Damascus steel has that pattern. I'm not a smith, but I know what I see.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: A local workshop sold it to me. They didn't say much. I assumed old stock. I paid fair, and I have a family to feed.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: Isn't it? Look closer if you like. The blade is on the stall.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: Still thinking? The blade won't stay here forever.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: You've been following my blade all over town, I hear. Ledger, forge, the lot. If you have something to say about my sign, say it in the square, where people can hear.

options.text: All right. In the square.
Not yet.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: New sign, Hesper's name on it. Funny thing: people trust it more. Two buyers asked about her other work. One asked about you. I told them {name} asked the maker first, and that {their} questions were fair.

options.text: Ask whether anyone left with the old sign’s words.
Ask what happened to the two slips.
Leave the stall.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: He looks at you for a long moment. 'You broke my sign in front of half the town. Now you want to write the new one?' He rubs the empty board. 'Fine. Something a buyer can check. Pattern-welded, Lyle workshop, this season. Short. If it does not sell, I will tell everyone whose idea it was.' For the first time since the market, he almost smiles.

options.text: Leave the stall.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: No sign today. I need time to think about what I write next. You were right about the steel. You did not have to be so loud about it.

options.text: Offer to help him write a sign that is true and still sells.
Ask whether anyone left with the old sign’s words.
Ask what happened to the two slips.
Leave the stall.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: I added the maker's name. That is as far as I go for now.

options.text: Can we talk in the square again?
Fair enough.
Ask whether anyone left with the old sign’s words.
Ask what happened to the two slips.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: The crowd liked my sign. Come back when you have more than questions.

options.text: I would like a rematch in the square.
Later.
Ask whether anyone left with the old sign’s words.
Ask what happened to the two slips.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: That blade on Corvan's stall? I made it. This season, in this forge. Pattern-welded: two steels, stacked, welded, twisted and folded.

options.text: Does that make it worse than wootz?
Can I try it myself?
Why didn't you label it?
You made it, so your view is biased. I will ignore it.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: Worse? No. Different. It's good steel and good work. But it is not wootz and it is not ancient. I want it called what it is.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: I sold it to Corvan with my sheet. He didn't keep the sheet. Traders and makers want different things from a label. Our values show in what we keep. I want my name and the season on that stall.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: Don't sort cards about it. Make it. Small billet, two routes: stack and weld, or melt in a sealed pot. Then cut it and take it to the assay table. Schematic only, mind. No real recipe.

options.text: Show me the anvil.
The anvil is just a tool. It does not change the result.
Later.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: The anvil is free whenever you want it. Try both routes if you like. Cut what you make and compare it at the assay table.

options.text: Use the anvil.
Goodbye.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: After the square I took out two tabs. See the square ink mark on each? In our shop it means I’ve taken on a repair. On the Nexus tab it means the counter took in a parcel. Here’s my marked scrap. Tie my tab to a bench slip and I can show which face I promised to mend. We’d need the bench for a bell. Send the tab with the scrap to the return drawer and anyone can ask for it at the counter. I can finish my turn here.

options.text: Yes. Come to the Nexus.
options.tag: Tie the repair tab to a bench slip

options.text: I'll ask Warden Ise first.
options.tag: Clip the repair tab to the drawer packet

options.text: Turn both tabs over.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: My initials and the face I promised to mend are on the back of the shop tab. We put the square in the corner so anyone working the bench can find a repair ticket with one hand. Your counter tab has a space for the arrival time. I could leave the blank one here all week and it wouldn’t get my scrap any nearer the Nexus.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: That knot will hold. I’ll bring the scrap and have your clerk date their tab when I arrive. My apprentice can cover the forge for one bell. I’ll cover their next turn when I get back.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: Clip it there, with my initials showing. Ask Ise to leave the drawer receipt beside it. People can check when the scrap reached the counter while I finish the forge turn. I’ll have to show the repair myself another day.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: Hold the scrap against the shop tab you tied. See how the two corners line up? This is the face I signed to mend. That square on the other tab goes with the clerk’s arrival time. Leave both on the peg. I’ll free the bench at the bell and get back to relieve my apprentice.

dialogue.speaker: warden-ise
dialogue.text: Unclip the marked tab beside the drawer receipt. Hesper signed for the face marked on her scrap. I put this bell’s time on the Nexus tab when it reached the counter. We can lend out both together. The bench is free and Hesper is still at her forge. Her demonstration can wait.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: I meant it. I want to see how you people test things. And I want to know where my stock really came from, now that you made me ask.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: The trade ledger? Every sale in Emberford goes in it. A Guardian with a Provenance Thread may read it. The desk is beside me.

options.text: Is the blade ancient, in your view?
Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: I've run this guild for thirty years. I know trade. I'd say a blade like that looks old. But I am a ledger man, not a smith.

options.text: If the guildmaster says so, it must be old.
What does the ledger say, though?

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: Careful. Trust me on prices and on who sold what to whom. On steel, ask the smith. My guess is just a guess.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: The ledger says what it says. Read it yourself at the desk. I don't argue with my own book.

options.text: So the ledger shows exactly what happened.
The guild's book is the only record we need.
Who writes in the ledger, and what goes unwritten?

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: The guild keeps trade peaceful. A quiet correction is usually better than a loud one. But that is a guild view.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: The market will remember how this was handled, one way or another.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: A Guardian! I am Sefa Okon. I keep the songs of Aethelgard, and I carry museum catalogues from your world. You're looking into the word 'Damascus'? It's a slippery word.

options.text: What is wootz?
Show me a real example.
What do the songs say?
I only want a source with no point of view at all.
Who catalogued the museum blades you carry?
On the coast I heard a story about this blade before I arrived.
I want to see how a pattern is made, not only read about it.
I know work songs from my valley too. Do your songs and mine agree?
Where I come from, steel with water patterns has another name.
Ask my own question.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: Wootz is a historical crucible-steel tradition. Not every crucible steel is wootz. And a pattern on the surface does not prove that a blade is wootz. I gave you a card on the two kinds of 'Damascus'.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: Here: the Met's record for ten wootz steel ingots with a bag. Catalogued as Indian, 'probably' eighteenth century. Keep the 'probably'. Open my catalogue on the table to read it.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: There is an Aethelgard work song: 'Look at the hand, not the shine.' It is our own song, made up for this world. It means: ask who made a thing before you praise its surface.

options.text: A song is only art. It cannot tell us anything.
Songs are not records. Only writing counts.
What does the song know that the ledger does not?
options.tag: Ask what a source can know

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: Ask, and I'll check my prepared topics.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: My catalogue is on the table. And you can still ask me a question of your own.

options.text: Ask my own question.
Who catalogued the museum blades you carry?
On the coast I heard a story about this blade before I arrived.
I want to see how a pattern is made, not only read about it.
I know work songs from my valley too. Do your songs and mine agree?
Where I come from, steel with water patterns has another name.
Goodbye.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: Emberford! Smell that forge. Talk to Corvan at the striped stall first. Then follow the blade's thread, and visit the smith.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: Kip is on his knees beside Corvan’s discarded sign. A tiny wax cricket sits in the thumb-sized nick. Every time he lifts the board it stops chirping. “Help me turn it. Look what was underneath.” A gold seal has stuck to the back.

dialogue.speaker: lumen
dialogue.text: Lumen’s light follows a ring pressed into the wood. “The seal fits the ring. My archive has no name for the hand that pressed it.” The cricket puts its feet back on the board and starts up again.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: Kip has one wax wrapper. “We could carry the shape. Or I could put my name and the hour inside. I was here when we found it. I was at supper when it was put up.” He sounds disappointed with himself. The cricket settles in the nick.

options.text: Let's take it to Ise. Press the wrapper round the nick.
Put the hour inside the fold. Let Kip sign where he found it.
It's just a tiny seal. Not worth showing Ise.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: The portal stone is ready. Let's take the seal to Warden Ise.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: Kip keeps working the seal’s shape into the palm of his mitten. “Ise stopped halfway to her pocket. Did you see? She usually puts things there before anyone can ask.”

options.text: Show me the wrapper we pressed.
Read me the hour again.
Leave Kip with his mitten.
Take a first rubbing from the discarded sign today.

dialogue.speaker: villager-1
dialogue.text: Ember tea? One mark. It doesn't make you smarter, but it makes the walk nicer.

options.text: Buy a cup (1 mark).
Any news in the market?
I found where the blade story began.
Any news today?
Read the tag on your kettle.
Did the night shift hear back?
Look at the folded account.
No thanks.

dialogue.speaker: villager-1
dialogue.text: Enjoy. Mind the forge sparks.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The Waystone by the fountain hums softly. Your progress is saved here. Rest is never required, and nothing is lost if you keep going.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Corvan's old sign board leans against the portal stone. Someone has scratched out most of the words.

dialogue.speaker: fruit-seller
dialogue.text: Have you heard? The blade on Corvan's stall came out of a king's tomb! Three people told me this morning.

options.text: Three people told you, so it must be true.
Who told the first of them?
Every story is as good as any other.

dialogue.speaker: fruit-seller
dialogue.text: Hm. They all heard it from the same man at the inn, now that I think of it. So it is really one story, told three times.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: The guild fair! Today's contest: two traders weigh the same sack of flour. One scale says 10, the other says 11. Which is right?

options.text: Test both scales with a known weight.
Take the average.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: The guild's brass standard weighs 5 on one scale and 5.5 on the other. One scale reads high. An average would hide that.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: A buyer wants a kitchen knife. I say it's worth 9 marks: six hours of work. She says 4: that is what a knife does for her. We are both being honest.

options.text: Who is right?
You are measuring different things.
It is just what each of you feels. There is nothing to discuss.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: We settled at 6, and she gets a free sharpening. A price is a meeting point, not a measurement.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: A child runs up with a coin from the mud. One side says EMBERFORD. The other side says OLD VELL. 'Which name is the real one?'

options.text: Maybe the town changed its name.
Ask Sefa, the song-keeper.
A name is just a label. It changes nothing.
The song about Old Vell is a myth, so the old name is false.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: Sefa looks at it: 'Old Vell was this town's name in the songs, before the guild came. Both names are real. They belong to different times.'

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Fog rolls in from the river. The landmarks disappear. You can still hear the forge hammer to the west and the fountain in the square.

options.text: Walk towards the sounds.
Wait for the fog to lift.
I cannot see anything, so I cannot know where I am.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Sound, slope and the smell of the forge are evidence too. The fog lifts after a few minutes. Nothing was lost.

dialogue.speaker: villager-1
dialogue.text: A Guardian! Here, take this town map. A traveller left a stack of them. Free.

dialogue.speaker: well-keeper
dialogue.text: The east well is low. My neighbour says the forge uses too much water. I say it's the dry season. We've argued all week.

options.text: What would you need to see to change your mind?
The forge must be the cause.
Asking the neighbours is just gossip. It is not evidence.

dialogue.speaker: well-keeper
dialogue.text: Hm. If the west well, far from the forge, is low too, it's the season. I'll go and look, and I'll take my neighbour.

dialogue.speaker: fruit-seller
dialogue.text: I remembered something. Last season a stranger sold Corvan his sign board. Polite. Wore a little gold ring. I didn't think about it until today.

options.text: A memory a week later can still be useful. Write it down with the date.
You only remembered now, so it can't be true.
I did not see the stranger myself, so I will not believe it.

dialogue.speaker: fruit-seller
dialogue.text: I'm not sure of the ring's colour, if I'm honest. Gold, I think. Put down 'I think'.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: I have a perspective, yes, and that is not the same as bias. I made it. That is also why I know how it was made. Don't trust me blindly: check me. Make a billet at the anvil and compare it with the blade.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: Then my shelves are empty. Every record was made by someone, for a reason. A museum catalogue too. What I can give you is records that you can check against each other. That is what objectivity looks like in an archive.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: Art carries what people noticed and cared about. 'Look at the hand, not the shine' tells you what buyers here were told to check for generations. The ledger never says that. When I travel, I sing that verse to let people hear a little of our workshop culture.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: The song-keepers check each other. A changed line is noticed at the next festival. And the song names the old smiths' marks. Hesper's mark is one of them. Check it on the blade yourself.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: The ledger knows who sold what, and when. The song knows what people here thought made a blade good. Two kinds of knowledge. Neither one is the whole story.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: It shows what a clerk wrote down. Sales, yes. Not the sheet that Hesper gave Corvan, and not what Corvan said at his stall. Ask the smith about the making.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: I like you saying that, but no. The song-keepers knew this town as Old Vell before the guild had a book. Sefa can tell you what the ledger never held.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: Our clerks write sales between guild members. Gifts, repairs and sales by outsiders often go unwritten. The book is honest about what it holds. It is silent about the rest.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: No? My anvil and my fire decide what I can make. A crucible needs a hotter, closed fire than I have here. The tool decides which blades exist, so it decides what you can test.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: “A thumb fits in there. Hesper says someone used to check whether the night hatch was open by touch. What if the board has had two jobs?” Kip waits. For once he has finished one question before starting the next.

options.text: Let's take it to Ise. Press the wrapper round the nick.
Put the hour inside the fold. Let Kip sign where he found it.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: The sign is one thing. In the morning I made slips for the runners. Someone kept one for a buyer who was already on the road. This is the spare. Order 27. It still says “ancient” in my hand.

options.text: Take the spare to trace where that claim went.
Leave the spare here for now.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: Orrin kept the order strip. The workshop chalked its terms on a slip of its own. Sefa put something by her catalogue that might help. I want every buyer to know which words were mine.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Order 27, trade desk. Corvan Hale bought one patterned piece from Hesper Lyle’s workshop in spring. The runner punched a hole beside 27 before taking a copy. This line dates a sale. It has no entry for the age of the stock.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: That piece was made here. Use my name or the workshop name so a buyer can find us. The hands at the bench agreed to tell you about their work, not to have their names read in the square. Keep that line of the slip folded.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: The Nexus sent me this account from the German patent office. It puts Loud’s patent apart from the practical pen and ink developed by the Bíró brothers and others. I would leave each account with the name of its own source. We can do the same with the maker’s words and that order.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: At the guild we file by order number. The runners start with a maker’s name, so people know whose words they carry. Some buyers can bring their copy here. Others only hear a runner before their cart leaves. Where do you want the first reply to go?

options.text: Pin a dated copy to Order 27 and carry a matching slip to the south gate.
Ask Hana and the runners to read the correction out, with Order 27 so buyers can check it.
Leave the slips on the board while I think.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: Here are two narrow slips with the same hole punch. One stays here so anyone can compare the two versions. Put the other on the small order table by the south gate. It needs to reach the people who took the original.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: Give the first copy to Hana at the west stall. Near a busy cart, “Hesper’s workshop made it here” will travel further than a long list of dates. Leave a slip with the order number there for the people who ask.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: A buyer at the south gate taps the old slip. “Ancient, it says. I never heard what happened in the square.” On her slip the order number is still legible. The ink after it has run in the rain.

options.text: Match the numbers and clip the dated correction beside her old slip.
Keep the copy with me for now.

dialogue.speaker: stallkeeper-hana
dialogue.text: The runner will leave with the ferry crew. He says he can carry the new words and still reach the far road by dark. The woman packing his load holds up an old slip. She has one question. “Who can I ask when you’ve gone?”

options.text: Let Hana read back the workshop’s words, then leave a copy with the order number.
Keep the slip and come back later.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The buyer turns both slips over and finds the matching punch. She crosses out “ancient” in her own copy. “I can still ask the workshop what we know about the stock,” she says, and takes both versions with her.

dialogue.speaker: stallkeeper-hana
dialogue.text: “Made here by Hesper’s workshop,” the runner repeats. “Order 27 at the guild.” The woman packing the cart takes a spare copy home. She stops the runner at the gate to make sure he remembers which part he can say out loud.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: A buyer came back with my old slip folded behind the reply. She wanted to see what had changed. I’m keeping both now. If a new buyer hears the old words, there’s a way back to us.

events.title: A rumour swarm
events.calm: A trader wants to tell you some gossip. You can listen now or later.

events.title: The weights-and-measures contest
events.calm: The guild fair has a short contest. Join it if you like.

events.title: A maker and a buyer
events.calm: Hesper and a buyer disagree about a price. They would like a third view.

events.title: A coin with two names
events.calm: A child has found a coin and wants to show you.

events.title: Fog over the market
events.calm: Fog will roll in for a few minutes. Nothing bad happens, and you can wait it out.

events.title: A free map
events.calm: The tea seller has something for you.

events.title: A low well
events.calm: Two neighbours disagree about a well. There is no hurry.

events.title: A late memory
events.calm: The fruit seller has remembered something about Corvan's sign.

hints.text: Step through the portal in the Nexus.
The portal opens after the new label holds.
Kip goes with you.
Walk onto the glowing circle at the north of the Nexus hall.
Corvan has a striped stall on the east side of the square.
Ask him what his sign claims, and why.
A seller's sign is a claim. Ask what it is based on.
Walk to Corvan, east of the fountain, and press E.
The Provenance Thread follows an object from hand to hand. Start where the blade is now.
Use the thread at the blade on Corvan's stall. Then look for the next place where the blade was recorded.
Sales in Emberford go in the guild ledger. The ledger desk is in front of the guild hall, to the north. Then the thread leads west.
Order: the blade on Corvan's stall, then the ledger desk next to Guildmaster Orrin, then the workshop sheet by Hesper's house in the west.
Hesper Lyle's forge is on the west side of town. Talk to her.
There are two routes: weld layers of two steels, or melt steel in a sealed pot. Try one, or both.
To finish a billet, cut it. Then take your section to the assay table, east of the square, and compare it with the blade's section.
At the anvil: Stack, Stack, Weld, Fold, Cut. Then go to the assay table and press 'Compare my billet'.
Corvan is ready to argue his sign in the square. Talk to him.
Each link in his claim can break. Which of your cards shows that a pattern can come from welding? Which one gives a date?
Ask for the source when he taps the gold mark. Challenge each link with a card that shows its limit. A careful claim is hard to crack.
Claim 'pattern-welded, Lyle workshop, this season'. Support it with the workshop sheet and the ledger. Challenge 'ancient' with the ledger. Concede that he paid fairly. Then rest.
Hesper watched the Showdown from the forge road.
She is back at her forge in the west.
Talk to her again.
Walk to Hesper in the west of town and press E.
Kip waits by the portal stone in the south.
He has found something.
Walk down the path south of the square.
Talk to Kip next to the glowing portal stone.
Step onto the portal stone to go back to the Nexus.
Warden Ise is in the centre of the archive hall.
Talk to Ise.
Stand on the portal stone, then walk to Ise in the Nexus and press E.
A stack of labels can outlast the loudest voice in the square.
The guild kept the order. The workshop kept its own terms. Sefa has seen a similar problem with records from the Nexus.
Look for the order strip near the guild desk, the chalk slip south of Hesper, and the archive packet beside Sefa.
Read all three slips. Compare the sale entry with the workshop’s permission, then see what Sefa leaves off her public caption.
Some of the people who need the correction will never stand at Corvan’s table.
A durable record and a message carried by people reach buyers in different ways.
Use the copy board near the guild after you check the three records. Hesper has approved the workshop’s name for either version.
Choose a dated copy buyers can match to their own slips, or have Hana and the runners read a shorter correction with the order number. Either keeps the workshop’s terms.
Find the people who left the square before the dispute ended.
The dated copy goes to the order table at the south gate. The spoken handover starts at Hana’s stall on the west side.
Your chosen route has a prop waiting for you. Look for the order table near the portal road or the relay slips one step southwest of Hana.
Use the south-gate order table and clip the correction beside the old slip, or use the west-stall relay slips and let Hana read back the correction.

moments.did: You brought a correction to someone who had already left with the old claim, while keeping the workshop’s permission.
moments.prompt: Who could still have the old version?
